title: How the Supreme Court Decides
short: Parties ask the Court to hear a case by a petition for certiorari; it takes a case when four justices agree (the rule of four); after briefs and oral argument the justices vote, and opinions are written for the majority, with concurring and dissenting opinions.
trouble: Students think a dissent has no effect. A dissent is not law, but later Courts sometimes adopt its reasoning; Harlan's dissent in Plessy is a famous example.

blocks.html: The Supreme Court sits at the top of the court system, but it does not have to hear most cases. Here is how a case gets there and how the justices decide it.

blocks.name: cv-order

items: A party loses in a federal court of appeals or a state high court
The loser files a petition for a writ of certiorari
At least four justices vote to hear the case (the rule of four)
Both sides file written briefs; others may file amicus ("friend of the court") briefs
Oral argument: lawyers answer the justices' questions, usually 30 minutes a side
The justices vote in a private conference
Opinions are written and announced, usually by the end of June

blocks.cap: The path of a case. Tap two steps to swap them, then Check.

blocks.html: Why choose cases? The Court is one court for a nation of hundreds of millions, so it spends its time where a ruling matters most: when courts of appeals disagree about what a federal law means (a "circuit split"), when a lower court strikes down a federal law, or when a question is very important. The rule of four is a custom, not a written law: four justices, one fewer than a majority, can put a case on the calendar. Turning down a case ("cert denied") does not mean the justices agree with the lower court; the lower ruling simply stands.

blocks.html: The Court hears a case when four justices grant certiorari. After briefs and oral argument the justices vote; the majority opinion is the law, while concurring and dissenting opinions explain other views.

blocks.title: Counting votes
blocks.q: Three justices want to hear a case and six do not. Will the Court hear it?
steps: The rule of four needs four votes to grant certiorari.
blocks.a: No. The lower court's decision stands, though that does not mean the Supreme Court approved it.

blocks.title: A dissent that came back
blocks.q: In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), the Court upheld segregated railroad cars 7 to 1. What happened to the dissent?
steps: Justice John Marshall Harlan wrote alone: "Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens."
His dissent was not law in 1896.
In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), the Court rejected "separate but equal" in public schools, and Harlan's dissent is often cited as having pointed the way.
blocks.a: It became a famous example of a dissent whose view later prevailed.

blocks.html: Thinking a dissent has no effect. A dissent is not law, but it can persuade later judges, lawmakers and the public. Check: ask "is this the opinion of a majority?" Only then is it the holding.
